entries.title: Chrome security fix
entries.lead: The browser now has the security fix Chrome released on November 9.

blocks.text: It closes a flaw in how pages handle XML that attackers were already using. How profiles look to sites does not change.

entries.title: Operating system version
entries.lead: Profiles could report Windows and macOS versions that were never released.

blocks.text: New profiles now get a version that exists, and a Mac profile gets one its chip can run. Profiles made earlier are corrected the next time the launcher starts. Linux profiles report no version, the way Chrome on Linux does.

entries.title: Touch screen
entries.lead: A profile without a touch screen showed this computer's touch screen to sites.

blocks.text: On a computer with a touch screen or a pen, such a profile reported touch input although its settings said there was none. It now looks like a computer with only a mouse. Profiles that claim a touch screen keep it.

entries.title: Dock icon
entries.lead: On macOS, clicking the Dock icon did not bring back a window closed to the menu bar.

blocks.text: It now does, as in other Mac apps. Clicking the icon in the menu bar opens its menu, as menu bar icons do on a Mac; Show Launcher is the first item.

entries.title: Extension updates in the API
entries.lead: The local API can now check for extension updates and install them.

blocks.text: For the whole library or one extension, with the same checks as the Extensions page, and with where each one stands: up to date, update available, waiting for a profile to close, or waiting for your approval. Updating them all never accepts new permissions; such extensions are left for you to approve. The API documentation in Settings describes the calls.

entries.title: Website address
entries.lead: Our website moved to shardx.com.

blocks.text: Links in the launcher and on the browser's start page now open shardx.com. New proxies made on the ProxyShard page use the shardx.com addresses; proxies you already have keep working.

entries.title: Android version number
entries.lead: Android profiles reported a Chrome version number that Chrome for Android never had.

blocks.text: Sites can compare it with the versions real phones run, and some, including ones protected by Akamai, flagged Android profiles for it. They now report the number of the Chrome for Android release.

entries.title: Android profiles
entries.lead: Android profiles showed a few features the way a computer has them, not the way a phone does.

blocks.text: They now match a phone in system accent colors, in-app purchases, saved offline content and barcode scanning.

entries.title: Video codecs
entries.lead: Sites saw this computer's video hardware, not the graphics card the profile claims.

blocks.text: Video support now matches the profile's graphics card and system, so a profile with an older card no longer reports formats that card cannot play. Profiles for macOS and phones, and cards the browser does not know, keep this computer's answers.
A profile can only lose formats this computer has, never gain new ones, so video keeps playing.

entries.title: WebRTC on one page
entries.lead: Behind a proxy, two WebRTC connections on the same page never connected to each other.

blocks.text: In Chrome they do, and some sites check this. Now they connect as in Chrome, and nothing between them leaves the browser. Where Chrome would show this computer's local address, the profile shows a made-up one that stays the same for the profile.

entries.title: WebRTC setup time
entries.lead: Behind a SOCKS5 proxy, WebRTC took 40 seconds to prepare a connection.

blocks.text: Chrome takes under a second, and sites can measure this. It now takes as long as in Chrome.

entries.title: WebRTC error address
entries.lead: Behind a proxy, a WebRTC error could show sites part of this computer's local address.

blocks.text: That part was the same for every profile on the computer. The error no longer shows any of it.

entries.title: Images a site draws
entries.lead: Images a site put on a canvas came back slightly changed, and the site could compare the two.

blocks.text: They now come back exactly as the site wrote them, as in Chrome. What the browser draws itself, such as text and shapes, still gets the profile's canvas noise.

entries.title: Canvas, WebGL and WebGPU reads
entries.lead: Reading one canvas image in different ways could give different results.

blocks.text: Some ways also returned it without the profile's noise. Every way of reading a canvas, WebGL or WebGPU image now gives the same result with the noise, as Chrome gives the same image every way.

entries.title: Maximized window
entries.lead: A profile's window can now open maximized, the way most people browse.

blocks.text: Turn on “Report the window as maximized” in the profile's Window settings. The window opens the size of the profile's screen, and sites see it maximized. Resize it, and sites see its real size. Phone profiles do not have this setting.

entries.title: Creation date in a team
entries.lead: Profiles in a team showed no creation date, so the list could not be sorted by newest or oldest.

blocks.text: The team server now keeps the date, and every member sees it, including members who may only see a profile.
Update the team server to 2.1.4 too. Profiles made before the update get their date the first time someone edits them from launcher 2.1.4.

entries.title: Proxies from ProxyShard
entries.lead: Proxies added on the ProxyShard page showed up in Proxies only after the launcher restarted.

blocks.text: They now show up at once, whether added from an order or generated.

entries.title: Banners on Windows
entries.lead: On Windows, the engine update and team banners ran under the window's minimize, maximize and close buttons.

blocks.text: The Try again button could end up under them and could not be clicked. The banners now end before the buttons.

entries.title: Chromium 157
entries.lead: Profiles now present themselves as Chrome 157, down to the network handshake.

blocks.text: The engine under every profile is now Chromium 157, and the version a profile reports moves with it: in the user agent, the client hints and navigator.userAgentData. The connection matches Chrome 157 as well, from the TLS handshake to the HTTP/2 settings, checked against a live Chrome 157.
The new engine downloads by itself the first time the launcher starts after this update. Profiles keep their data, and the version they report is updated at their next start.

entries.title: WebRTC on a proxy without UDP
entries.lead: On an HTTP proxy, or a SOCKS5 proxy without UDP, a page could learn this computer's real address through WebRTC.

blocks.text: A page could hand the browser back its own local network name, or make it send to an address of the page's choosing. Now WebRTC sends no UDP past such a proxy at all, and local names are not answered behind any proxy. This holds for starts from the launcher, the API and the SDKs.
TURN servers over TCP or TLS now work through the proxy, so a page that asks for a relay gets a real one, reached from the proxy's address.

entries.title: Languages in a removed frame
entries.lead: A frame already removed from the page reported the profile's whole language list, where Chrome reports one language.

blocks.text: Some bot protection checks exactly this and turned the browser away, for example on qrator.net. A removed frame now answers the way Chrome does. Frames on the page and workers still report the full list.

entries.title: WebGPU reads
entries.lead: Pixels copied out of WebGPU and read back carried no canvas noise, so they came out the same in every profile on one computer.

blocks.text: They now get the same marks as WebGL, from the profile's seed. Reading the same image twice gives the same result, and reading part of it matches the whole.

entries.title: Fullscreen in synced windows
entries.lead: Chrome 157 keeps a window that isn't in focus from going fullscreen, which would have held back the synchronizer's other windows.

blocks.text: Synced windows still follow the leading one into fullscreen. Everywhere else the new rule applies, as in Chrome.

entries.title: Profile name in the browser
entries.lead: The profile's name next to the address and in the window title can now be hidden.

blocks.text: Turn off “Show the profile name in the browser” in Settings. The home button with your page stays. From the SDKs, pass hideProfileName in Node or hide_profile_name in Python and Rust.

entries.title: Profile password
entries.lead: A profile can now be protected with a password of its own.

blocks.text: Turn on “Protect profiles with a password” in Settings, then set a password when you create a profile or from its menu. It is asked at every start. While the profile is closed, its browser data, fingerprint and proxy are kept encrypted; only its name, folder and tags stay readable.
A forgotten password can't be recovered, and without it the profile can't be opened.

entries.title: Camera and microphone on Mac
entries.lead: On a Mac, sites saw the camera and microphone but got no picture and no sound.

blocks.text: macOS asks for access on behalf of the launcher, and the launcher never asked, so the system refused without a word. Now macOS shows its usual request the first time a site uses the camera or microphone. Allow it once and both work in every profile.

entries.title: Cache of deleted profiles
entries.lead: Deleting a profile left its browser cache on disk.

blocks.text: The cache now goes with the profile, including profiles removed from the trash, temporary profiles and team copies. Cache left behind by profiles deleted earlier is cleared once, at the first start after this update.

entries.title: Bookmark folders
entries.lead: Bookmarks imported from Chrome all landed in one flat list.

blocks.text: Folders now come over as they are in Chrome, and the profile gets the same layout: the bookmarks bar on its bar, other bookmarks in Other bookmarks. A site kept in several folders stays in each, and bookmarklets are imported too. The Bookmarks page has a Bookmark folder column to sort and search by.

The ShardBrowser folder leaves profiles at their next start: bookmarks made in the launcher sit on the bookmarks bar itself. Bookmarks imported before this update land there in one flat row; to get their folders, delete them and import the file again. Bookmarks you add inside a profile are never moved or removed.

entries.title: Deleting many bookmarks
entries.lead: Bookmarks could only be deleted one at a time.

blocks.text: Select bookmarks, or all of them with the box in the header, and delete them in one go. Selection follows the search and the folder tab, and Undo brings them all back. The folder tabs above the list now scroll with the mouse wheel when they don't fit.

entries.title: Select all
entries.lead: The select-all box in the header of Profiles, Proxies and Trash appeared only once something was already selected.

blocks.text: It now shows as soon as the pointer is over the list.

entries.title: Automation on an open profile
entries.lead: Starting automation for a profile that was already open failed with an error in English.

blocks.text: If the profile is open without automation, the launcher offers to restart it: it closes the normal way and reopens with its tabs. If it is already running with automation, the automator connects to it. While a project run is driving the profile, the launcher says so instead.

entries.title: Installing the engine ahead of time
entries.lead: The SDKs can now install the browser engine before the first run.

blocks.text: Run shardx install in Python (python -m shardx install works too) or npx shardx install in Node; --force reinstalls and --cache-dir picks the folder. This suits Docker images. In Rust, call install on the runtime.

entries.title: Closing from the SDKs
entries.lead: On Windows the SDKs ended the browser abruptly, so what pages had just saved could be lost and sites could log out.

blocks.text: Closing a session now asks the browser to quit the normal way first, as the launcher does, on every system.

entries.title: Protected video module
entries.lead: The module that plays protected video told sites this computer's real operating system and processor.

blocks.text: A site can ask it for a license request without playing anything, and that request carried this computer's system, processor and device details, whatever the profile claimed. It now works the way it does in Chrome, and the first request carries none of them. Protected video plays as before.

entries.title: WebGL 1
entries.lead: WebGL 1 answered some settings that only WebGL 2 has, and listed its extensions in a different order than Chrome.

blocks.text: Asking WebGL 1 for a WebGL 2 setting now returns the same error as in Chrome, and extensions come in Chrome's order. The values the profile sets are unchanged.

entries.title: Fonts of another system
entries.lead: A profile of another system showed this computer's fonts, such as Mac fonts in a Windows profile on a Mac.

blocks.text: Such a profile now has the fonts of the system it claims: a Windows profile has Segoe UI, Calibri and Consolas and no Mac fonts, and a Mac profile on Windows the other way round. Text is drawn with the closest fonts this computer has, so letter widths are still this computer's.
Profiles of the same system as the computer are unchanged.

entries.title: Processor in calculations
entries.lead: Some calculations give different results on Apple chips and on Intel or AMD processors, and profiles gave this computer's.

blocks.text: A Mac profile on a Windows or Linux computer, or a Windows profile on a Mac, now gives the results of the processor it claims. Profiles on a computer with the same kind of processor work exactly as before.

entries.title: Screen in headless mode
entries.lead: In headless mode pages were drawn on a small screen at normal scale, whatever screen the profile claims.

blocks.text: Pages are now drawn on the profile's screen at its scale, so text and emoji measure the same as in a window. This works for starts from the launcher, the API and the SDKs.
A screen you pass yourself with --screen-info is used as given.

entries.title: WebGPU on Apple profiles
entries.lead: macOS profiles with Apple chips lacked one WebGPU feature that Chrome reports on those Macs.

blocks.text: New profiles have it, and existing ones get it at their next start. Nothing else in the profile changes.

entries.title: Teams
entries.lead: Share profiles with the people you work with, through a server you run yourself.

blocks.text: Run the team server on any Linux machine and invite members from the Team page. Rights are given per team, folder or profile: see, start, edit, delete, cookies, take out. A profile is open on one computer at a time; when it closes, its cookies and logins return to the server for the next person.
The admin doesn't need to be online. Removing a member ends their access at once. Deleted items stay in the team's Trash for 30 days.

entries.title: Sync between your computers
entries.lead: Your own profiles, proxies and the rest follow you to your other computers.

blocks.text: Connect it in Settings to your own server or your team's, then turn it on for the profiles you want. They travel with their sessions, proxies, folders, tags, bookmarks, extensions and automation projects. Launcher settings and the fingerprint library stay on each computer.
A profile open on one computer can't start on another until it closes there. Offline changes go out when the server is back; if a profile changed on two computers, both versions are kept.

entries.title: Extension updates
entries.lead: Extensions added from the Chrome Web Store show when a new version is out and update in place.

blocks.text: The launcher checks every few hours, or now with Check for updates. Updating keeps the extension's data, such as wallets and logins. If profiles using it are running, the update waits until they close, and a version asking for more access asks you first.
Extensions added earlier need one Link to Web Store… from their menu.
The check uses this computer's own connection, as Chrome does. It can be turned off in Settings.

entries.title: Bookmarks from Chrome
entries.lead: Import the Bookmarks file of a Chrome profile into the launcher's bookmarks.

blocks.text: Choose the file on the Bookmarks page, pick which profiles the bookmarks show in, and import. Folders from Chrome come in as one list, duplicates and bookmarklets are skipped, and importing the same file again adds nothing. Chrome shows where its Bookmarks file is on chrome://version.

entries.title: Large screens
entries.lead: Lists and pages use the whole window, and the interface size can follow the screen.

blocks.text: Tables stretch across the window instead of leaving an empty band on the right, and the Team, Settings and ProxyShard pages are no longer a narrow column. The new Auto interface size picks a larger size on large screens such as 4K.

entries.title: Screen size for new Windows and Linux profiles
entries.lead: A new Windows or Linux profile starts with this computer's screen size.

blocks.text: On these systems the screen depends on the monitor, so the profile's window now matches the screen it reports. macOS and Android profiles keep the screen of their device. Any size can still be picked by hand, and existing profiles keep theirs.

entries.title: Browser interface language
entries.lead: Each profile can show the browser's menus in your language or in the profile's.

blocks.text: Fingerprint › Browser interface language: System language (the default) or Same as the profile language. Pages see the profile's language either way.

entries.title: An engine update that did not finish
entries.lead: A failed engine update no longer leaves the launcher without a browser engine.

blocks.text: If the download breaks, the disk is full, or profiles are still running, the current engine stays and keeps working. A notice at the top says what stopped the update and offers to try again; when profiles are in the way it can close them and finish. An update that already downloaded finishes without downloading again.

entries.title: Cookies kept when a profile stops
entries.lead: Stopping a profile could lose cookies set in its last half-minute.

blocks.text: Stop now closes the browser the normal way on every system, so everything it had is saved, even when a page asks “Leave site?”. The same goes for profiles closed when you quit the launcher.

entries.title: Creating a profile
entries.lead: On some computers New profile kept loading and never opened the form.

blocks.text: The form no longer waits for the graphics check of this computer. The check runs once in the background, and the compatibility badges appear when it finishes.

entries.title: Data folder on an external drive
entries.lead: With the data folder on an external drive, the list of profiles could fail to load.

blocks.text: macOS leaves hidden service files on such drives, and the launcher tried to read them as profiles. They are now skipped everywhere.

entries.title: Sort order on Windows
entries.lead: On Windows the sort list in the Display menu did not open.

blocks.text: Clicks inside the Display and Filters menus could start moving the window instead. They now reach the menu. In Russian, the column hint “appears when a tag is created” no longer covers the column name.

entries.title: Long lists in pickers
entries.lead: At 90% interface size a list did not scroll to the selected or last item, and a notice could cover the bottom rows of the proxy list.

blocks.text: Lists scroll to where they should at every interface size, and notices move out of the way of an open list. Arrow keys move through a list even while the pointer rests on it.

entries.title: New bookmark from a folder tab
entries.lead: A bookmark created on a folder tab was saved so that no profile showed it.

blocks.text: It is now saved for that folder, the same as when the folder is picked in the form.

entries.title: ShardBrowser everywhere
entries.lead: The launcher and the browser's start page now say ShardBrowser, and About links to shardbrowser.com.

blocks.text: The Russian translation was also reworded where it read like a word-for-word translation; Views are now called «Сохранённые фильтры» in Russian.

entries.title: Closing the last tab on macOS
entries.lead: Closing a profile's last tab on macOS no longer stops the profile.

blocks.text: The browser stays open in the Dock, the way Chrome does on a Mac, and the launcher keeps showing it as running. Quit, Cmd+Q or Stop in the launcher end it. Show the window in the launcher opens a new window when none is left.

entries.title: Extension welcome pages
entries.lead: Extensions such as MetaMask and Authenticator opened their welcome page at every start.

blocks.text: The browser treated them as freshly installed each time. Now that happens once per profile, and what extensions set up for later, such as reminders, survives a restart. Their data was never lost.
Welcome tabs that piled up before this update stay until you close them once.

entries.title: Extensions installed inside a profile
entries.lead: Extensions installed from the Web Store inside a profile were hidden while the profile also had extensions from the launcher.

blocks.text: Both kinds now work side by side. Extensions installed inside a profile were not removed before, only hidden, so they come back with their data.

entries.title: Extensions from other programs
entries.lead: Programs on this computer that add extensions to Chrome could add them to profiles too.

blocks.text: Profiles now ignore extensions registered for Chrome on this computer. Only extensions you add in the launcher or inside the profile are used.

entries.title: One language for the whole profile
entries.lead: Some parts of the browser still answered in this computer's language instead of the profile's.

blocks.text: Extensions now see the profile's languages, so MetaMask and Phantom agree. Pages without a declared text encoding, dates and numbers follow the profile's language the way Chrome in that language does. On macOS profiles speech voices are named in the profile's language.
MetaMask and Phantom keep the language they picked at first start. If already installed, switch it once in their settings — don't reinstall them, that removes the wallet.

entries.title: Sound a page plays back
entries.lead: Audio protection also changed sound a page had written itself and read back unchanged.

blocks.text: Some checks compare a sound before and after the browser handles it. Sound a page wrote is now returned exactly as written, and protection applies only to sound the browser computes itself.

entries.title: An extension-only object on web pages
entries.lead: Web pages could see an object that ordinary Chrome shows only to extensions.

blocks.text: Detection services look for it. It is no longer available to web pages; extensions keep it.

entries.title: Human Type on mobile profiles
entries.lead: On mobile profiles the right-click menu had no Human Type and fill items.

blocks.text: A long press now offers them, and they type into the field you pressed on.

entries.title: Dropdowns filled by Shard Helper on Windows and Linux
entries.lead: Fill left standard dropdowns empty on Windows and Linux.

blocks.text: Shard Helper now picks the option the way a person does: it opens the list, moves to the option and confirms it, then checks the field took the value. If the page moves while it fills, it aims at where each field is now.

entries.title: Freezes on Linux
entries.lead: With Shard Helper on, the browser on Linux could freeze while starting and left a crash report on every start.

blocks.text: Both are gone. Real crashes are still recorded as before.

entries.title: The browser engine moves to Chromium 156
entries.lead: Profiles now present themselves as Chrome 156, down to the network handshake.

blocks.text: The engine under every profile is now Chromium 156. The version a profile reports moves with it — in the user agent, in the client hints and in navigator.userAgentData — so profiles don't fall behind the Chrome that real visitors run.

The connection matches Chrome 156 too: the TLS handshake, including the GREASE value among the signature algorithms and the Trust Anchor IDs extension that Chrome 156 now sends, the HTTP/2 settings, and the default Accept header with image/jxl. A site that compares the version a browser declares with the way it connects sees the same browser in both.
The new engine downloads by itself the first time the launcher starts after this update. Profiles keep their data.

entries.title: A new launcher interface
entries.lead: Every page was redone: profiles open in a side panel next to the list, and Folders, Tags and Views keep large fleets in order.

blocks.text: Click a profile to see and edit it in Peek, the panel beside the list, without leaving the list. Folders group profiles, Tags mark states such as “warm-up” or “needs 2FA”, and a View saves a filter, a sort and a set of columns in the sidebar. Press Cmd+K (Ctrl+K) to reach any command or profile by typing.

The app is now called ShardBrowser Launcher. On macOS the new version installs next to the old one: once it opens, delete “ShardX Launcher” from Applications. Both use the same data, so nothing has to be moved.

entries.title: Changes wait for Save
entries.lead: Nothing is written while you type; leaving a page or quitting with unsaved changes asks first.

blocks.text: Profiles, proxies, settings and automation projects keep your edits until you press Save. Quitting from the menu, the tray or Cmd+Q asks whether to save them, discard them or stay.

entries.title: Delete all data
entries.lead: Settings › Storage can start the launcher over without losing anything.

blocks.text: Profiles, proxies, automation and settings move into a backup folder beside your data, together with Tags, Views and Folder colors. Nothing is deleted, and an interrupted reset offers to undo or finish at the next start. The browser engine and the fingerprint library stay.

entries.title: Residential traffic history
entries.lead: The ProxyShard page charts how much residential traffic you used and how many requests went through.

blocks.text: Pick the last 24 hours, 7 days or 30 days: each residential plan shows its traffic over that time and how it compares with the period before. Datacenter and ISP proxies have no traffic limit, so they have no chart.

entries.title: Window size for profiles that named none
entries.lead: A profile without a window size opened as large as this computer's screen allows.

blocks.text: The window is now taken from the screen the profile declares and stored with the profile on its next start, so it opens inside its own screen. On Windows and Linux a resolution you pick for a profile is no longer replaced by the “real screen” setting, which is meant for macOS profiles.

entries.title: Proxies that differ only in password
entries.lead: Importing the same gateway with different session passwords kept only the first.

blocks.text: Providers put a sticky session or a country into the password, so one host, port and user can be many different exits. Each password is now its own proxy; only an exact duplicate is skipped.

entries.title: Cancel a profile that is still starting
entries.lead: A profile waiting on a slow proxy can be canceled before its browser opens.

blocks.text: Cancel stops the start before the browser window appears, instead of letting it open and closing it again.

entries.title: Canvases that came back unmarked
entries.lead: On some profiles the most commonly probed canvas was handed over exactly as the computer had drawn it.

blocks.text: Canvas protection marks the picture a page reads back. On some profiles those marks were landing where they made no difference, and the page ended up with the canvas exactly as this computer had drawn it. Because the marks follow from the profile, such a profile did it every time, not now and then.

Marking now covers the canvases fingerprinting libraries actually draw. Measured across twenty profiles on the shapes those libraries use, every profile hands back a canvas of its own and none matches an unprotected browser. What you see on screen is unchanged.

entries.title: A filled rectangle read back exactly
entries.lead: A page could fill a rectangle inside a canvas it had drawn on, read it back, and find pixels that did not match the color it asked for.

blocks.text: A canvas filled entirely with one color was already handed back untouched. A rectangle inside a canvas with other things on it was not, so comparing that rectangle against the color it was filled with found around 26 pixels in 8000 that differed — a difference no ordinary browser produces.

A pixel surrounded on all sides by its own color is now left alone, which covers any rectangle filled with one color wherever it sits. The decision ignores the bit a mark would change, so marking one pixel cannot change the answer for the pixel beside it, and it is taken from the whole canvas rather than from the rectangle being read — otherwise reading a canvas whole and reading it in quarters would disagree, which is itself a check pages run.

It costs little: text and gradients have hardly any pixel with a 2 by 2 square of its own color around it, so a 220 by 30 text canvas still carries 27 to 42 marks and a plain background with one word on it 3 to 15 — enough for a canvas unique to that profile, which is checked rather than assumed.

A canvas asked for in floating point is covered the same way now. Saving one as an image used to skip the marks entirely, so the same drawing was protected when read as pixels and not when saved as a file.

entries.title: WebGL pictures that changed between reads
entries.lead: Reading the same WebGL canvas twice gave two different pictures, and two profiles could give the same one.

blocks.text: The noise added to a WebGL canvas was tied to how many times it had been read rather than to where the pixels are, so a page that read it twice and compared got a different answer each time — and that difference is itself the answer: something is editing this canvas. The profile's own number was not reaching the WebGL path at all, which is why two profiles could produce identical pictures.

Marks now belong to a position in the drawing buffer, the way they already did for an ordinary canvas, and they come from the profile. Reading the whole canvas, reading a corner of it and saving it as a file now agree, and two profiles no longer agree with each other.

Two things kept the ways of reading apart even after that: a WebGL buffer is handed over bottom row first, and a canvas snapshot on macOS stores blue before red. Both are accounted for, and the agreement was measured rather than assumed.

A page can ask WebGL to leave gaps between the rows it reads, or to skip the first few. The marks ignored both, so they landed on the wrong pixels and the picture read back stopped matching the one an export produced. They follow the page's own layout now.

entries.title: SVG element sizes that disagreed
entries.lead: An SVG shape reported one size through one call and a different size through another.

blocks.text: Element measurements carry a small amount of noise so the exact font metrics of this computer cannot be read off them. One SVG-only way of asking for a size went around it, so a page could ask twice and get two answers. The same went for the size reported when an SVG element changes size.
All three now go through the same calculation and return the same numbers.

entries.title: The language of form error messages
entries.lead: A form that refused what was typed explained why in the computer's language, not the profile's.

blocks.text: The text the browser itself puts under an invalid field — the "please fill in this field" kind — came from the language the program was installed in. A profile set to Polish on an English computer answered in English, which no ordinary browser in that configuration would do. The message now follows the profile's language.

entries.title: Clicks inside embedded frames on a mobile profile
entries.lead: On a mobile profile a click never reached a frame embedded from another site, reCAPTCHA among them.

blocks.text: A mobile profile reports a screen and a window of its own, and the coordinates of a click were being translated into that reported window twice — once for the page and again for anything embedded in it from a different site. The second translation moved the click off the frame entirely, so the checkbox never saw it. The translation now happens once, and a click lands where it was aimed whatever frame it belongs to.

entries.title: The browser after the last window closes
entries.lead: On macOS the browser kept running with no windows open, and the profile stayed marked as running.

blocks.text: Closing the last window on macOS normally leaves the application running — that is how the platform works — but for a profile it meant the launcher went on showing it as running, and starting it again attached to the leftover instead of opening a window. The browser now exits with its last window, which is what a profile is for.

entries.title: Location updates repeating without end
entries.lead: A page asking to be told when the location changes was told over and over, forever.

blocks.text: A profile declares one fixed location, so there is nothing to report after the first answer. The code that delivered it kept rescheduling itself anyway, which left a page receiving the same coordinates several times a second and the processor busy producing them.

entries.title: Keeping a background window focused
entries.lead: A page can tell its window is not the one in front, which matters when several profiles run at once.

blocks.text: Sites check whether their window is the active one, and a window sitting behind another honestly says it is not. With a row of profiles working at the same time only one of them can be in front, so a profile can now be told to report itself as focused regardless.
Off by default, and deliberately so: a window that is always focused is itself unusual if nothing else about the profile explains it. Turn it on for profiles that work in the background.

entries.title: The voices a profile offers
entries.lead: Every profile offered the same voices, taken from the computer it was running on.

blocks.text: The list of speech voices a browser can offer is one of the longer things a page can read, and it follows from the operating system and its language. Ours was the computer's own list, so a Polish Windows profile on an English Mac offered Mac voices with English names.

A profile now offers the voices its declared system and language would have: the Windows roster for a Windows profile, the built-in set for macOS, and an empty list for Linux, which is what a Linux machine without extra packages really reports.
The first voice in the list is the default one, which is how Chrome decides it, and Windows voice names are not translated — the system stores them in English whatever the interface language is.

entries.title: A window larger than the screen it declares
entries.lead: A profile could report a window that did not fit on the screen it said it had.

blocks.text: The window and the screen are declared separately and nothing kept them consistent, so a profile claiming a 1366 by 768 screen could open a 1920-wide window on it. Any page that compares the two finds a shape no real computer produces. The window is now held inside the declared screen, and the space the system bars take is counted the way the declared system would count it.

entries.title: Proxy logins with special characters
entries.lead: A proxy whose user name or password contained a colon, an at sign or a percent failed to connect.

blocks.text: Those characters have a meaning inside a proxy address, so a password containing one was read as the end of the password and the start of something else. The address is now assembled so the characters are carried rather than interpreted — in the browser, in the launcher and in all the SDKs — and the reverse step reads addresses written either way.

entries.title: Processor load on an idle window
entries.lead: A window with nothing happening in it used a steady 200% of processor time.

blocks.text: A profile reports a window position of its own, and the part of the browser that tells the page where its window is was being given that reported position and then comparing it against the real one. They never matched, so it asked again, every frame, for as long as the window stayed open.
The reported values are now handed to the page without being written back, and the comparison is against what the window really is. The page still sees the position the profile declares.

entries.title: Measurements that sat between pixels
entries.lead: Every length a page measured came back a fraction off the step browsers actually use.

blocks.text: Element sizes carry a small amount of noise so that the exact widths of this computer's fonts cannot be read off them. The noise was a free-floating fraction, and that put the answer where no browser puts it: a plain element reported 137.00392150878906 where every real browser reports 137. A page could see at a glance that the number had been altered.
Measurements now land where a real browser puts them, each kind on the footing it belongs to, so a length reads as an ordinary number instead of announcing that something changed it.

The amount is the size of an ordinary layout rounding: enough to change what a fingerprint adds up to, small enough that nothing moves on screen and a page comparing a measurement against its own stylesheet sees what it expects.

entries.title: The shape of measured text
entries.lead: Measuring text on a canvas returned the width through the profile and the shape of the letters straight from the computer.

blocks.text: A text measurement hands back a dozen numbers. The width was going through the profile; the four that describe the box the letters actually ink — how far they reach left, right, up and down — were not, and they say as much about which font this computer has as the width does. A page reading them got the real answer out of the same call whose width was protected.
Those four now carry the profile's own step, each keeping the step it sits on, and a letter with nothing below the line still measures exactly zero below the line.

entries.title: A WebGL surface cleared to one color
entries.lead: Clearing a WebGL surface to a color and reading it back returned pixels that were not that color.

blocks.text: An ordinary canvas filled with one color was already handed back untouched; the WebGL side of the same rule was missing, so the simplest check anyone can write — clear to a color, read the pixels, compare — came back with a scattering of pixels one step off. A flat area drawn inside a WebGL scene had the same problem.
A pixel surrounded by its own color is now left alone there too, and reading the surface back through the drawing interface agrees with saving it as an image, pixel for pixel.

entries.title: Sizes a page chose itself, handed back changed
entries.lead: A page could set an element's size, measure it, and see a number that was not the one it asked for.

blocks.text: Element sizes carry a small amount of noise so the exact widths of this computer's fonts cannot be read off them. It was applied to every measurement, including the ones where the page itself decided the answer: a box set to 400 pixels wide came back as 400.015625. Nothing about this computer is in that number — the page wrote it — so changing it hid nothing and told the page the measurements were being altered.

Only sizes the fonts decided are covered now. A size pinned in the stylesheet comes back exactly, whether it was pinned outright, by a smallest and largest that meet, by a percentage of a pinned parent, or by fixing both edges of a positioned box. A box as wide as its own text — a line, a word, a cell stretched by the text beside it — still is.

Three more ways of reading one rectangle used to disagree with each other and now do not: observing an element's size handed back the untouched box, the parts of a wrapped line no longer add up to something other than the whole, and an element under a transform reports exactly the transform applied to it.

entries.title: A start page of our own
entries.lead: New tabs and the home button open a page that says what the browser does.

blocks.text: It is built into the browser at `chrome://shardx` and asks nothing of the network — no fonts, no images, no counters — so it opens at once, offline, and tells nobody that it was opened. It follows the system's light and dark setting.

entries.title: Bringing a running profile's window to the front
entries.lead: There was no way to get back to a profile's window from the launcher.

blocks.text: Clicking the *Running* badge in the profile list now raises that profile's window, on all three systems. The same thing is available over the API and in the SDKs, so a script that opened a dozen profiles can bring any of them forward.

entries.title: A running profile shown as idle on Windows
entries.lead: On Windows a profile that was open showed as idle in the list.

blocks.text: The launcher noticed the browser process had ended, but on Windows the browser hands its work to a second process and leaves, so the window was still there with nothing watching it. It now waits for the profile's own lock to be released, which is the thing that actually says the browser is gone.

entries.title: A variable in the wait step
entries.lead: The *Wait* step in automation would not take a variable for how long to wait.

blocks.text: Every other step accepted a variable in a number field; this one read the field as a plain number and stopped on anything else. It now resolves a variable the way the rest do.

entries.title: Reporting the computer's own processor and memory
entries.lead: A profile always reported invented hardware, even where the real figures would have been safer.

blocks.text: A profile normally declares a processor count, an amount of memory and a graphics card of its own. When the profile's operating system is the same as this computer's, reporting the real ones is both consistent and harder to argue with, so the profile editor now offers *Real* for each of them.
Only offered when the systems match, and never chosen for you: a Windows profile reporting a Mac's graphics card is worse than any invented pair.

entries.title: Profile icons
entries.lead: Profiles fell back to the stock icon, and the badge drawn on it was hard to read on a dark Mac.

blocks.text: A profile without a picture of its own used the application's icon, which made a row of profiles indistinguishable in the dock and in the window switcher. It now gets a generated icon carrying its color and initials. The badge that marks it was redrawn so it reads on both the light and the dark macOS appearance.

entries.title: The proxy checker
entries.lead: Dead proxies were reported as working, with no address to show for them, and the check took a long time.

blocks.text: The check stopped at the handshake, and a proxy that accepts a connection and then refuses to carry anything passes that. It now opens a real connection through the proxy to a known address and asks what address came out the other end: a proxy that cannot carry traffic fails, and a working one reports the address it presents.

Three other things were making it slow or wrong. A secure address was being probed in plain text, which some proxies answer and some hang on. A probe with no deadline could hang for minutes. And results were written where a later check overwrote them, so a proxy tested twice lost its first answer. Each step now has its own deadline, the whole check has one, and results are kept per proxy.
Checking a proxy without UDP support is no longer slow: it used to wait out the full UDP timeout before concluding, and now concludes as soon as the proxy says it does not support it.

entries.title: Copying a profile's debugging address
entries.lead: Attaching a script to a running profile meant finding its debugging address by hand.

blocks.text: A profile started with debugging enabled now offers *Copy debugging address* in its menu, which puts the address on the clipboard ready to paste into a script.
A page can tell when a developer tool is attached to it, so use this with care on work a site is not meant to see as automation.

entries.title: An interrupted engine download
entries.lead: A download that broke off part way left the computer with no browser engine at all.

blocks.text: The old engine was deleted before the new one had been fetched, so a dropped connection left nothing to fall back on and nothing to run. The new engine is now downloaded first and the old one replaced only once it is on disk — in the launcher and in all three SDKs, which each carried their own copy of the same mistake.

The same step also wrote a fixed engine version into the profile list when it could not reach the network, so profiles claimed a version the installed engine did not have. It now reports what is actually installed.

entries.title: Checking the launcher from a script
entries.lead: A script could not tell a launcher that was not running from one that refused its key.

blocks.text: Both failures looked the same from outside, which made them hard to act on. There is now a health check that says which it is, and a way to find a profile by its name rather than by its identifier.

entries.title: Changing a proxy password over the API
entries.lead: Updating a proxy password through the API added another proxy instead of changing the one in use.

blocks.text: Each change left another entry behind with the profile still pointing at the old one, so a fleet accumulated dead proxies and went on using the password that no longer worked. The change is now applied to the entry the profile actually uses.

entries.title: Russian in the launcher
entries.lead: The launcher now speaks Russian.

blocks.text: Everything the launcher itself says — menus, settings, the profile editor, automation steps and error messages — is available in Russian, alongside English and Chinese. Change it in *Settings*.
This page stays in English whatever the launcher is set to.

entries.title: A trial of premium residential
entries.lead: The Proxies page offers a free trial of premium residential traffic while no ProxyShard account is connected.

blocks.text: How much traffic the trial is for, and whether there is one at all, is decided by ProxyShard rather than by the launcher, so the offer can change without an update. Taking it opens your browser; the traffic lands in the account you sign in with. Connect an API key afterwards and your orders, traffic and proxies appear on that page.
Nothing is shown when there is no offer, and nothing is shown once a key is connected.

entries.title: Turning a device in a script
entries.lead: The SDKs could not reach the commands that rotate the screen or move the sensors.

blocks.text: A profile started from an SDK was missing the switch that opens those commands, so a script could set up a mobile profile and then not turn it. Every SDK now starts the browser with it and attaches to the page's own session, so rotation, motion and the rest answer the same way they do from the launcher.

entries.title: An empty clipboard
entries.lead: Importing from an empty clipboard reported a system error instead of saying it was empty.

blocks.text: Nothing to paste is not a failure. It now says so plainly, and the import stays where it was instead of closing.

entries.title: Arrow keys after moving to another page
entries.lead: On every page but the one the launcher opens on, the arrow keys did nothing until a row was clicked.

blocks.text: Moving to Proxies, Bookmarks or Fingerprints puts the keyboard on the page's heading, and a list only answered the arrows when the keyboard was on nothing at all. Lists now take the arrows from the heading as well, so one can be walked straight after switching pages, without reaching for the mouse first.

entries.title: Canvas readings that disagreed with each other
entries.lead: A page could prove the canvas was being altered by comparing two ways of reading it.

blocks.text: A page can read a canvas as an image or as raw pixels, and the two must match — the image format is lossless, so any difference means something is being added in between. Ours differed, on a handful of pixels, every time. Comparing the two is a standard check, and it was passing back a definite answer: this browser edits its canvas.

The marks were placed at byte positions inside whichever buffer was at hand, and a canvas snapshot stores colors in a different order than raw pixels do, so “the first color” meant blue on one path and red on the other. The position also depended on the rectangle asked for, so reading a canvas whole and reading it in quarters disagreed as well. Marks now belong to a point on the canvas rather than to a place in a buffer, and the color is chosen as a color.

Two more ways out of the canvas carried no noise at all — saving it as a file rather than as an address, and the same call from a canvas running off the main thread — and a third, reading it back as floating point, quietly returned the untouched picture. All of them are marked now, in the same place and the same way.

A mark only goes where it survives being read back: on a see-through pixel the stored color is always zero, so a mark there would be a pixel no ordinary browser can produce. Translucent pixels are marked wherever the arithmetic returns the same byte, which also means a page cannot switch the whole thing off by drawing everything at 99% opacity. The smallest canvas worth marking is now judged by area rather than by each side, so the short wide surfaces detectors actually use — 220 by 30 and the like — are covered again.

entries.title: The audio fingerprint that never changed
entries.lead: Every profile on a machine reported the same one, whatever seed it had.

blocks.text: A page fingerprints audio by rendering a tone through a compressor and adding up 500 of the resulting samples. Our noise moved each sample by the smallest step a number of that kind can take, in a direction as often down as up — so across 500 samples the changes canceled and the total came out the same to more decimal places than anyone reads. Noise off, seed A, seed B: one number, and the same number on every machine running the browser.

The step is larger now, chosen so the total lands where two real machines running the same Chrome already differ from each other. Across a thousand seeds, every one produced a different total and none matched the untouched one. The change is far below anything audible. The profile's audio intensity setting, which until now was read from the profile and then used by nothing, sets how far they move.

The live spectrum readings had a fault of their own: the value taken from each byte depended on one bit of the profile's seed, so every profile on a machine fell into one of two answers. Over four thousand seeds that produced two distinct patterns; it now produces three and a half thousand. And digital silence stays digital silence — it used to come back as 129 where every real browser answers 128.

A page reading a buffer in small pieces now costs what the pieces cost. Marking ran over the whole buffer on each of those calls, so a library streaming 44100 samples in chunks of 128 walked the buffer 344 times, and how long that takes is itself something a page can measure.

entries.title: Half of all profiles had no noise at all
entries.lead: Seeds above a certain size were thrown away, and canvas, WebGL and element measurements went unprotected.

blocks.text: Each profile gets its own random number to drive its canvas, WebGL, audio and element-measurement noise. The launcher draws that number from the full 32-bit range; the browser read it into a slot half that size, so every value above 2147483647 was read as “not set”. Roughly one profile in two therefore ran with no noise at all while its settings said the noise was on — the same canvas hash as a plain browser, and the same as every other such profile on the machine.

The whole range is read now. Profiles that were affected start producing their own canvas, WebGL and rect values from the next launch — which is a change to their fingerprint, and the point of the fix. The same reading mistake was fixed for the WebGPU limits, where a real graphics card reports numbers right at that boundary.

entries.title: How often the screen refreshes
entries.lead: A 240 Hz gaming monitor was measurable inside every profile on the machine.

blocks.text: There is no property a page can read for this, but there is a clock: ask the browser to draw a frame and time how long it waits. That wait was the real monitor's. On a 240 Hz screen every profile answered 240 — a rate a few percent of desktops have, identical across every profile on that computer, and sitting next to a claimed graphics card no such panel is sold with.

A profile now carries a refresh rate of its own and the browser holds its frames to it. 60 unless the profile says otherwise, which is what most machines report; pick another in the profile editor, next to cores and memory, or set screen.refresh_rate through the API.

The rate can only be lowered — a computer cannot draw faster than its own panel. On macOS frames come from the display itself and can only be answered or skipped, so the claim is met when the panel divides down to it exactly: 60 out of 60, 120 or 240 is exact, and those are nearly every machine. A claim the panel cannot divide down to is left at the panel's rate rather than answered with something like 48 Hz, which no display ships and which would be a worse thing to be than honest.

entries.title: A WebGL read that wrote past the end of the page's own array
entries.lead: Reading pixels in any format other than RGBA bytes wrote four bytes per pixel into a smaller buffer.

blocks.text: The WebGL noise assumed every readPixels hands back four bytes per pixel. A page reading a single-channel framebuffer — gl.readPixels(..., gl.RED, gl.UNSIGNED_BYTE, buf) — passes a buffer a quarter of that size, and the noise wrote the full four bytes per pixel into it, past the end of memory the page owns. It now asks the same routine that validated the call how large the buffer really is, and leaves any read that is not RGBA bytes untouched.

entries.title: Profiles in a folder with a non-English name
entries.lead: On Windows the browser could not read them and ran on the real machine instead.

blocks.text: If the path to the profile contained anything outside the English alphabet — a Windows user folder named in Russian, Chinese or Portuguese is enough — the browser read that path as empty, failed to open the file, and started anyway. Everything a page asked was then answered by the real computer: its graphics card, its screen, its processor. Nothing on screen said so.

The path is read in full now. And a profile that was asked for and could not be loaded is written into the log as an error saying the browser is about to report its real hardware, rather than a line nobody would find.

entries.title: Extension popups opening full screen
entries.lead: A wallet popup asking for 360 by 600 got the size of the whole display.

blocks.text: A profile's window is sized to the screen the profile claims, and that size was being applied to every window the browser opened — including the small ones extensions ask for. Solflare and anything like it opened the size of the display.

Two things now have to be true before that size is used: the window has to be an ordinary browser window, so a popup, an app window or devtools keeps what it asked for; and nobody may have asked for a size already. An extension calling chrome.windows.create with a width and a height but no type gets an ordinary window carrying explicit bounds, and those bounds are the caller's answer, not ours to overwrite.

entries.title: WebRTC on a SOCKS5 proxy
entries.lead: A profile behind a proxy had no WebRTC at all — no address, no candidates, nothing.

blocks.text: WebRTC sends its own UDP, and on a proxy that UDP goes through the proxy's relay. Opening the relay takes a moment — on a mobile proxy about a second and a half. WebRTC starts asking for data before that, and the socket answered those first reads with a hard failure. The layer above treats a hard failure as the socket being gone: it tears it down and does not build another. So the relay came up a second later with nothing left to use it, for the whole life of the tab.
What a site saw was a browser that gathers no candidates. Not a hidden address — no WebRTC at all, which is its own kind of answer, and not one any ordinary browser gives.

Reading is no longer tied to the relay being ready: the read waits, and the first packet through arrives on it. Sending before the relay is up reports the destination as temporarily unreachable, which is a normal thing for a UDP socket to say and which the layer above already knows how to wait out. With a mobile proxy bound, all three STUN configurations now return the proxy's exit address.

entries.title: HTTP/3 and WebRTC sharing one relay on a proxy
entries.lead: Only the first socket through the proxy worked. The others sent fine and heard nothing, and their answers arrived on the first one.

blocks.text: UDP on a SOCKS5 proxy goes through a relay the proxy opens on request. The browser is allowed to leave its own address out of that request, and the proxy then takes whichever socket speaks first and serves only that one from then on. We opened a single relay and ran everything through it — every HTTP/3 connection and every WebRTC port.

So the first socket worked and the rest did not. Their packets went out normally, nothing came back, and the replies were delivered into the first socket instead, where they read as packets belonging to a connection they had nothing to do with. On a page opening HTTP/3 to more than one site that is one connection failing for no visible reason, and which one it is changes from load to load. WebRTC had the same shape: a call needing more than one port had one working port and the others silent.

Each socket now opens a relay of its own. Two spares are kept connected ahead of time, because the first handshake against a mobile proxy takes about a second and a half — a connection that had to wait for one would lose the race to ordinary HTTPS every time and never be used.

Separately from this: whether HTTP/3 runs at all still depends on the proxy letting UDP out on port 443. On one mobile proxy two channels of the same host behaved differently — one carried QUIC, the other answered nothing on 443 while carrying UDP fine on other ports. When it is blocked the browser tries HTTP/3, gets no answer and carries on over HTTPS, which is what a phone on that network does too.

entries.title: WebGL1 offering extensions it cannot hand over
entries.lead: Two calls, no permission needed, and the list gave itself away.

blocks.text: WebGL1 and WebGL2 do not have the same extensions: sixteen names exist only in the first because the second folded them into the language, and seventeen only in the second. A profile carrying a single list handed that one list to both, so a WebGL1 context advertised names it could not return — a page asks getSupportedExtensions(), asks getExtension() for one of them, gets null, and has learned in two steps that the list was not written by a driver. The other half was quieter and worse: nothing was pinned for WebGL2, so the real driver's list went out there.

Profiles that carry one list are now split as they load, each context losing the names it cannot have, so older profiles are fixed where they sit with nothing to regenerate. The split follows the browser's own registration lists rather than a table written by hand. Profiles that already declare both are used exactly as written.

entries.title: The screen a profile declares, on Windows and Linux
entries.lead: Every profile on one machine reported that machine's monitor, whatever screen it was given.

blocks.text: A profile's screen was replaced with the host display on every start. That was meant as a clamp — a window cannot be larger than the monitor it opens on — but outside macOS it ran even when the declared screen fitted easily. On a 5120 by 1440 monitor every profile said 5120 by 1440: one unusual pair, shared by the whole fleet, which is the opposite of what a per-profile screen is for.

The declared screen is now kept whenever the real display can hold it, on every platform, and the clamp is left for the case it was written for. A profile created through the API with 1920 by 1080 keeps 1920 by 1080.

entries.title: The timezone a profile starts on
entries.lead: A geo lookup that fails now tries the others, and never falls back to your own clock.

blocks.text: The location of a proxy was read from one service only. ip-api, the default, has no HTTPS on its free tier, so a proxy that refuses plain HTTP failed on it and nothing else was tried. The launcher then fell back to this computer's own timezone and language without telling anyone — the one thing a profile must never show.

All three services are tried now, the chosen one first, and the two others speak HTTPS. A service over its daily quota answers with an ordinary-looking 200 carrying an error inside, which used to count as a successful lookup that simply found nothing; that now counts as a failure and the next service gets its turn. When a proxy has no location the Test panel says why, on the proxy itself.

And a profile behind a proxy no longer starts on this computer's clock at all. It starts on UTC, with a message on screen rather than a line in a log — UTC is wrong, but it is nobody's address. Without a proxy the host's own timezone is right, and on Windows the launcher can finally read it: it used to look only where Linux and macOS keep it, find nothing, and settle on UTC for every profile.

entries.title: A settings file that cannot be read
entries.lead: One stray byte used to wipe your settings and sign out every API client.

blocks.text: If anything went wrong while reading settings.json, the launcher quietly carried on with an empty set: the API off, its port at zero, the helper and the camera off, the theme blank. It then wrote that emptiness back to disk along with a fresh API key, so every token you had issued stopped working. A byte-order mark was enough — PowerShell writes one whenever you edit the file with Set-Content, and a plain redirect writes the file in an encoding the launcher did not read at all.

Now a file that cannot be read is left exactly as it is. The launcher runs on defaults for that session, says so at the top of Settings, and keeps your API key. Saving from that screen is refused while the file is unreadable, with a message saying why — because what is on screen are defaults, and writing them would replace whatever the file holds, the location of your profiles among them. Byte-order marks and UTF-16 are read correctly now, so the usual cause is gone.

entries.title: Saving over someone else's change
entries.lead: The editor no longer reverts what the API changed while it was open.

blocks.text: Open a profile in the editor, change it from a script through the API, then press Save: the editor wrote its own copy over the top and your script's changes were gone, with nothing said. Every profile now carries a version number, and the editor remembers the one it opened. A save that would land on a newer version is refused, and the message tells you to reopen the profile and apply your changes to the current one.

The number only moves when the profile itself changes. Launching a profile records the time it started and closing it records how long it ran; neither is something an open editor disagrees with, and counting them would have refused your own save while blaming an API nobody had called.

entries.title: “On startup” in the browser
entries.lead: A profile continues where it left off, and the setting decides — the launcher stopped overruling it.

blocks.text: Whatever you picked under “On startup”, the profile always reopened the tabs from last time. The launcher was passing “restore the last session” on every start, which overrides the setting, so “Open the New Tab page” could be checked and never take effect.

The switch is gone and the answer moved to where it belongs. A profile now continues where it left off by default, and a choice made in settings is stored on the profile and wins over that default. Both entries do what they say, and nothing has to be checked to keep the behavior you already had.

Profiles made before this carry an explicit “New Tab page” that nobody chose — it was the browser's own default at the time and got written into the profile, so a new default alone would not reach them. That one value is now cleared once, on the next start, and the profile continues where it left off like the rest. A profile holding anything else picked it deliberately and is left alone, and this runs once: pick the New Tab page after it and it stays picked.

entries.title: The debugging address on start
entries.lead: Starting a profile through the API waits longer for the address, and says why when it has none.

blocks.text: Starting a profile through the API sometimes answered with no cdp object, and the address turned up in the log a few seconds later. The wait was six seconds, which a cold start on Windows with a large profile can outrun. It is thirty now. When even that is not enough the answer carries a cdp_error saying what happened and where to read the address yourself, instead of leaving you to guess from a missing field.

entries.title: The Python SDK on Windows
entries.lead: Profiles with non-English text no longer break the SDK.

blocks.text: On Windows the SDK read and wrote its files in whatever encoding the system happened to use, while every file it touches is UTF-8. A profile carrying a Spanish voice name, a Chinese one, or a note in Russian ended the first example in the README with UnicodeDecodeError. Worse in the other direction: the fingerprint handed to the browser was written in the local encoding, so those names reached it damaged. Every read and write is UTF-8 now.

entries.title: Chinese in the launcher
entries.lead: Every screen, switchable in Settings and picked up on its own on a Chinese system.

blocks.text: There is a Language setting at the top of Settings. On a system already set to Chinese the launcher starts in Chinese without being asked. It is the launcher's own text only — what language a site sees is the profile's, and that has always been separate.

1479 pieces of text, covering every screen: the profile list and its editor, proxies and the ProxyShard pages, the automation project editor with its whole step library, extensions, bookmarks, the fingerprint library, the trash and settings, along with every message, prompt and confirmation they raise.

The text lives in shared/i18n/locales/en.json and zh.json under names like profileTable.lastRun, so rewording the English touches one line in one file instead of every place it is shown, and another language is one more file. `npm run check:i18n` fails the build if a new string is added without one, if a key is called that no locale has, or if the two files drift apart.

entries.title: Refresh rate in the profile editor
entries.lead: Pick the rate the profile's screen claims, next to its cores and memory.

blocks.text: The browser learned to hold its frames to a rate the profile names, and the editor is where you name it: a Screen refresh rate list under CPU and memory, with the rates real panels ship with. 60 unless you change it, which is what most machines report.
Frames can only be slowed down. A profile asking for more than this computer's own screen quietly runs at the screen's rate, so on a 60 Hz machine there is nothing above 60 to claim.

entries.title: Ordering the profile list
entries.lead: By name, by age, by when it last ran, or by how much it has been used.

blocks.text: The list only ever came in the order profiles were added. Under Filters there is now an Order setting: name A→Z or Z→A, newest or oldest first, last launched, or most used. It is remembered between restarts, and selecting a range with shift follows what you see rather than the old order.

entries.title: Cookies in the profile editor
entries.lead: Pick a cookies file while making the profile instead of afterwards.

blocks.text: Loading cookies meant creating the profile, finding its row and using the menu. The editor has a Cookies block now: pick the file there and it is loaded the moment the profile is saved. Same JSON array as before, and the same rule — the profile has to be stopped, which a profile being created is.

entries.title: The icon in the macOS menu bar
entries.lead: It follows the light and dark bar instead of staying purple.

blocks.text: The launcher put its full-color mark in the menu bar, where every other icon is a plain stencil that turns dark on a light bar and light on a dark one. It is drawn from the mark's shape now, the way macOS expects.

entries.title: The UDP test with a VPN running
entries.lead: A VPN could make the launcher decide a working proxy had no UDP, and start profiles with QUIC and WebRTC switched off.

blocks.text: Before starting a profile the launcher checks whether the proxy can carry UDP, and turns QUIC and WebRTC off when it cannot. The check was one probe: send a packet, wait for an answer. It could not tell apart a proxy with no UDP and a computer that could not send the probe in the first place.

Some VPNs filter UDP per application. On one of those the launcher's probe got nothing while the browser on the same machine, at the same moment, went through the same proxy without trouble. The proxy was fine; the launcher's own packet never left. Every profile then started with QUIC and WebRTC removed.

The launcher now checks whether it can send UDP from this machine at all before reading anything into the result. When it cannot, it says so and leaves the profile alone rather than deciding on the proxy's behalf.

entries.title: Finger gestures outside the desktop app
entries.lead: The touch steps existed only in the Automation editor. Nothing outside it could tap, swipe or turn a phone.

blocks.text: A phone profile has no cursor, and the browser enforces that: it refuses pointer commands on a phone and finger commands everywhere else. The Automation editor knew this and had the gestures — tap, long press, swipe, drag, pinch. Nothing else did. Over MCP an agent driving a phone profile got a refusal from every click and every field it typed into, with nothing to say why. The SDKs had no input layer at all, and neither the API reference nor the read-me mentioned any of it.

The gestures are now on every surface. MCP gained six tools — tap, long press, swipe, drag, pinch and rotate — and the existing human ones stopped needing to be told which kind of profile they are on: on a phone a click becomes a tap, a right click becomes a long press, and filling a field taps it first. Moving the cursor is the one that still refuses, because hovering has no touch equivalent and a tap in its place would be a different thing that looked like it worked.

Fixing that turned up a second thing: over MCP the human pointer and typing had never worked at all. The input domain is built from the tab behind the session, and the server was asking for one that has no tab, so every human click and every human keystroke came back "no live frame" — on desktop profiles too, not only phones. It now asks on the page.

All three SDKs gained the input domain, pointer and finger both. The API reference lists the touch steps with their parameters, and the read-me describes the whole domain, including the parts that were already there and undocumented — scrolling with the device the profile's platform implies, and pressing a named key through the profile's own keyboard layout.

Turning the screen is new everywhere, including the editor, where it is the Rotate screen step. The turn is physical: the sensors move first and the picture commits at the end, the order a real handset produces. A profile with no motion sensors refuses it — a device with no accelerometer cannot notice it has been turned.

entries.title: Every preset showing a GPU mismatch
entries.lead: The check that reads this machine's GPU asked on a page where the answer is never available.

blocks.text: The launcher starts the engine once to learn what the host GPU can do, and compares presets against it. It asked on a blank page — and WebGPU is only exposed on a page with a real origin, so the question came back “there is no adapter here”. That was written down as fact: no adapter features at all, and every preset in the library then looked like it claimed more than the machine had.

The check now runs on a real page and gets the real answer. An empty adapter list is also no longer accepted as one: a working machine does not report zero features, so that is a question that failed, and it is asked again next time instead of being cached until the engine version happens to change.

entries.title: Screen resolution in the profile editor
entries.lead: On Windows and Linux you can now pick one, and only sizes this monitor can actually show are offered.

blocks.text: A resolution list sits under the refresh rate for Windows and Linux profiles, defaulting to whatever the fingerprint carries. The list stops at this machine's own monitor: a window cannot be larger than the screen it opens on, so a bigger claim is contradicted by the window the moment a page reads it.

The available area keeps the fingerprint's own inset — the strip a taskbar or menubar occupies — rather than being invented, because a screen whose usable height equals its full height is a screen with no system chrome, which no ordinary desktop has. macOS has no such control: there the profile's own screen was already kept as written.

entries.title: Fonts on a mobile profile
entries.lead: A profile claiming a phone reports the fonts that phone has, and none of the machine's own.

blocks.text: A page learns which fonts you have by measuring text, and a phone profile used to measure the fonts of the computer it was running on — a page could find Apple Chancery, or Segoe UI, on a device that has neither. The profile now carries the device's own set, and that set is all a page can find.

Names the device really has answer as present even when the machine has no such file, because the browser draws them with a face it does have. What cannot be reproduced is the exact shape of the letters: the widths are the stand-in's. A detector holding a table of real widths can still tell; one asking which fonts exist cannot.

The set is written as groups, because a phone's font configuration mostly is: on Android, Arial, Helvetica, Tahoma and Verdana are one file, and a page measuring all four gets one width. Android profiles carry their maker's own fonts too — Samsung, Motorola, OnePlus, Xiaomi and vivo each add their own.

entries.title: WebGPU on a Linux profile
entries.lead: A profile claiming Linux gave the machine's own graphics adapter away.

blocks.text: Chrome on Linux ships with WebGPU switched off, so a page asking it for an adapter is answered with nothing. Ours answered with the adapter of the machine it ran on — vendor "apple", architecture "metal-3", beside a WebGL string naming an NVIDIA card on a Mesa driver. It now answers with nothing, the way Chrome on Linux does. navigator.gpu stays where it is; it is the adapter request that comes back empty.

entries.title: Protected video on Android profiles
entries.lead: An optional switch for the video a phone can play and a desktop cannot.

blocks.text: Almost any current phone plays protected video at a level no desktop offers, and a site that checks gets a different answer from a profile claiming a phone. Turn on Media in the profile editor and the profile claims it. It is off by default and only offered on mobile profiles, because the claim is only as good as the machine behind it: a site that takes it up will ask for video this computer may not be able to decode.

entries.title: Turning the screen
entries.lead: A mobile profile can be turned, and everything turns with it.

blocks.text: Over the debugging port, Motion.setOrientation turns the claimed screen. The screen, the window, the media queries a page lays itself out with and the motion sensors all follow — and the sensors travel through the turn the way a hand does rather than jumping, because a device that arrives at a new angle without having moved is not a device.

entries.title: Dragging with a finger
entries.lead: A new step for carrying something across the page, where a swipe only flicks it.

blocks.text: A swipe scrolls; a drag moves the thing under the finger. The finger now rests long enough for the page to decide it is a drag and not a scroll, then travels from where it came to rest — which is what a slider, a map or a sortable list needs. Automation reaches it as Motion.touchDrag, and the launcher's own drag step uses it on a mobile profile.

entries.title: Graphics features in profiles
entries.lead: Profiles carry the WebGPU features of the device they were taken from.

blocks.text: A page can list those features in one call, and a list belonging to a different card than the one the profile names is a contradiction. Every profile in the library now carries its own, and the browser never reports more than the machine can actually back.

Fixed along the way: the warning about a feature your machine cannot provide was shown for every profile at once, because the list of what this machine supports had been recorded before there was anything to record. A missing record is no longer read as "supports nothing".

entries.title: Mobile profile
entries.lead: A profile claiming a phone now reports one consistently: its connection, orientation, fonts and motion sensors all agree with the device it says it is.

blocks.text: The connection block takes raw values now — the ones the device would have measured — and the browser rounds them the way it rounds real ones. A profile pinning 75 ms used to report exactly 75, which no Chrome reports, and the same number to every site. Add "type" to name the link, for example "cellular4g".

Screen orientation follows the screen the profile already sets, so a portrait phone no longer says landscape. There is no separate setting for it, on purpose: a second place to state which way the device is held is how the two ended up disagreeing.

Fonts match what a phone has: the local font list is gone, the decorative generic families collapse onto the default as they do on Android, and text scaling works. Page text may render slightly differently on a mobile profile as a result.

Motion sensors report a device being held. Add "motion": { "carry": "hand" } — or "table" or "walking" — to choose how much it moves. Without them a page listening for movement heard nothing at all, which no phone does.

entries.title: Touch
entries.lead: A profile can now claim a phone, and the browser behaves like one: your mouse and wheel reach the page as finger touches, not as a cursor.
